title: Rutherford IIa — Marginally Threatened
disclaimer: For professional education and simulation only. Not for direct patient-care decision-making.
synthetic_findings: Mild sensory loss limited to the toes

stages.title: Stage 1: Initial recognition and focused assessment
stages.narrative: A synthetic patient develops sudden unilateral lower-limb pain. The limb is cooler than the opposite side, and a pedal pulse is not palpable.
stages.question: What is the most appropriate immediate educational priority?
stages.rationale: Sudden limb pain with perfusion findings should trigger urgent vascular assessment focused on symptom timing, limb viability, sensory and motor function, and arterial and venous Doppler signals.
stages.safety_principle: Acute limb ischemia is time-sensitive; assessment of limb viability and neurologic function should not be deferred.

choices.text: Initiate urgent vascular assessment with focused sensory, motor, pulse, and Doppler examination
choices.feedback: This promptly establishes limb viability and the urgency of the synthetic presentation.

choices.text: Arrange routine outpatient review after a period of home observation
choices.feedback: Routine follow-up is inappropriate for a time-sensitive acute ischemic presentation.

choices.text: Provide analgesia and reassess only if pain persists the next day
choices.feedback: Symptom relief alone does not establish limb viability or address possible progression.

choices.text: Limit the initial assessment to evaluation for venous thrombosis
choices.feedback: A venous differential may be considered, but restricting the assessment misses the arterial emergency pattern.

stages.title: Stage 2: Rutherford classification
stages.narrative: Focused examination shows mild sensory loss limited to the toes, no motor weakness, an absent arterial Doppler signal, and a preserved venous Doppler signal.
stages.question: Which Rutherford category best matches these synthetic findings?
stages.rationale: Sensory loss limited to the toes without motor deficit, with absent arterial but preserved venous Doppler signals, is consistent with a marginally threatened Rutherford IIa limb.
stages.safety_principle: Motor weakness or sensory loss extending beyond the toes may indicate progression toward Rutherford IIb and greater urgency.

choices.text: Rutherford I — Viable
choices.feedback: A viable limb has no sensory loss; this synthetic case already has toe sensory change.

choices.text: Rutherford IIa — Marginally threatened
choices.feedback: The limited sensory deficit, preserved motor function, and Doppler pattern support Rutherford IIa.

choices.text: Rutherford IIb — Immediately threatened
choices.feedback: Rutherford IIb generally includes a more extensive sensory deficit and motor weakness, which are absent here.

choices.text: Rutherford III — Irreversible
choices.feedback: Profound anesthesia, paralysis, and absent arterial and venous signals are not present.

stages.title: Stage 3: Immediate management
stages.narrative: The synthetic limb remains Rutherford IIa and salvageable with prompt treatment. No contraindication to anticoagulation has been identified.
stages.question: Which immediate management bundle best reflects the educational pathway?
stages.rationale: The immediate pathway combines urgent vascular-surgery assessment, intravenous unfractionated heparin unless contraindicated, analgesia and supportive care, prompt anatomical imaging when it will not cause harmful delay, and repeated neurological and vascular reassessment.
stages.safety_principle: Bleeding risk and anticoagulation contraindications must be checked, and any new motor weakness or expanding sensory deficit requires immediate escalation.

choices.text: Arrange urgent vascular-surgery assessment; give intravenous unfractionated heparin unless contraindicated; provide analgesia and supportive care; obtain prompt anatomical imaging if it causes no harmful delay; and repeat neurological and vascular assessments
choices.feedback: This addresses thrombus propagation, comfort, anatomical planning, specialist escalation, and surveillance for deterioration.

choices.text: Withhold all antithrombotic therapy until every imaging study is complete
choices.feedback: Routine delay can permit thrombus propagation; contraindications should drive withholding, not imaging completion alone.

choices.text: Apply compression and encourage ambulation as the primary treatment
choices.feedback: This does not address acute arterial occlusion and may delay appropriate escalation.

choices.text: Discharge for observation because motor function is preserved
choices.feedback: Preserved motor function defines IIa rather than absence of threat; urgent assessment and management remain necessary.

stages.title: Stage 4: Diagnostic imaging and treatment planning
stages.narrative: The synthetic presentation remains stable after initial assessment, and anatomical definition can be obtained without delaying escalation.
stages.question: What is the best imaging and planning principle?
stages.rationale: Prompt anatomical imaging can guide the limb-salvage strategy in a stable Rutherford IIa presentation when obtaining it will not create harmful delay, while neurological and vascular status continues to be reassessed.
stages.safety_principle: Imaging supports treatment planning but must not delay escalation if the limb progresses toward Rutherford IIb.

choices.text: Obtain prompt anatomical imaging and use it to plan treatment, provided it causes no harmful delay
choices.feedback: This balances anatomical definition with the time-sensitive nature of limb salvage.

choices.text: Schedule elective imaging the following week before deciding whether escalation is needed
choices.feedback: Elective delay is inconsistent with a threatened acute limb.

choices.text: Avoid anatomical imaging in every Rutherford IIa presentation
choices.feedback: Anatomical information often helps select an appropriate limb-salvage approach when it can be obtained promptly.

choices.text: Commit to one treatment modality before considering anatomy or cause
choices.feedback: Treatment selection should account for the occlusion pattern, etiology, duration, and available expertise.

stages.title: Stage 5: Definitive management and escalation
stages.narrative: Imaging defines an occlusive lesion. Sensory loss remains limited to the toes, motor function remains intact, and the venous Doppler signal is preserved.
stages.question: Which definitive strategy best reflects a guideline-grounded case-conference discussion?
stages.rationale: Selection among catheter-directed thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, surgical thromboembolectomy, bypass, or hybrid treatment is individualized to anatomy, etiology, symptom duration, bleeding risk, comorbidity, and local expertise.
stages.safety_principle: New motor weakness or expanding sensory loss suggests progression to Rutherford IIb and requires immediate escalation.

choices.text: Select catheter-directed thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, surgical thromboembolectomy, bypass, or a hybrid strategy according to anatomy, etiology, symptom duration, bleeding risk, comorbidity, and local expertise while reassessing for IIb progression
choices.feedback: This recognizes the available limb-salvage modalities, the factors that guide selection, and the need for active surveillance for worsening threat.

choices.text: Use the same revascularization procedure for every Rutherford IIa presentation
choices.feedback: No single modality is appropriate for every anatomy, etiology, comorbidity profile, or local capability.

choices.text: Observe without further neurovascular reassessment because the initial category was IIa
choices.feedback: Rutherford status can evolve; loss of motor function or worsening sensation changes urgency.

choices.text: Treat primary amputation as the routine first strategy for a salvageable Rutherford IIa limb
choices.feedback: Rutherford IIa is salvageable when promptly managed; routine primary amputation does not match this category.
